title: Born from above (John 3:1–8)
hook: Nicodemus comes by night; the wind blows where it will
carry: the wind blows where it will

segments.voice: Yesterday, naos: Jesus called his own body a temple. Your line was a temple of flesh.

Some conversations only happen at night. The kitchen at one in the morning. The question you'd never ask in daylight, in front of people. John tells of a man who came to Jesus by night: Nicodemus, a Pharisee, a respected teacher, a leader among his people. He has a reputation, and he has questions. Maybe he comes in the dark to avoid being seen. Maybe for a quiet hour. John doesn't say. But John has already told us the light shines in the darkness.

Nicodemus opens politely: "Rabbi, we know that thou art a teacher come from God." Jesus answers something he didn't ask: "Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." The Greek word translated again, anōthen, means two things: again, a second time, and from above. Nicodemus hears the first: "How can a man be born when he is old? can he enter the second time into his mother's womb, and be born?" He's not being foolish; he's taking the words at face value. But Jesus means the second as well: a birth that comes from God, of water and of the Spirit. Then an image from the weather: "The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit." In Greek, wind and Spirit are the same word, pneuma. You can't grab the wind or schedule it. You only hear it in the trees and feel it on your face. Christians understand this new birth in different ways. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican teaching connects water and the Spirit closely with baptism. Evangelical preaching speaks of being born again as a personal turning to Christ, often a moment a person can name. Both read Jesus as pointing to a life that starts from God.
screen: `HOW CAN A MAN BE BORN WHEN OLD?`
then, large: `THE WIND BLOWETH WHERE IT LISTETH.`

segments.voice: Open a window or step outside if you can; if not, notice the air moving in the room, or your own breath. Feel it on your face and hands, and listen for it in leaves or against the glass: you can't see it or hold it, but it's plainly there. If you pray, ask God's Spirit to move in you like that; if you don't, let the air remind you that some things are real without being held.
Anothen, the Greek word that means both from above and again — Jesus's double meaning for Nicodemus: a second birth that comes from God, by water and the Spirit, as free as the wind.
Your line: the wind blows where it will. You can hear it, even when you can't hold it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Churches that baptize infants link Jesus's words to Nicodemus with baptism, and in evangelical churches being 'born again' describes a personal commitment to Christ; some Christians hold both together.

fork.setup: you're Nicodemus. a teacher tells you that unless you're born again you can't see the kingdom of God. what do you ask?
options: how can a man be born when he is old?
fork.reveal: "how can a man be born when he is old?" he hears 'a second time'. Jesus means 'from above': a birth of water and the Spirit.

original.note: Greek: from above, and also again, anew. the double meaning that Nicodemus misses.

chat.says: What does 'born again' actually mean? I've only ever heard it as a label.
options: Jesus's word means both again and from above: a new life that starts from God.
A fresh start you make by willpower alone, like turning over a new leaf.
Just a label one church uses; it has no real root in what Jesus said.
chat.meaning: Jesus's Greek word, anothen, means both again and from above: a birth that comes from God, of water and of the Spirit.

Nicodemus.meaning: a Pharisee and leader who came to Jesus by night

pneuma.meaning: Greek for both wind and Spirit

notes: Why Nicodemus came by night is unstated; two possibilities are offered without choosing. Confirm.

Views on new birth: baptismal regeneration (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, many Anglicans) and conversion experience (many evangelicals). Confirm each is fairly described, and that many hold both together.
ἄνωθεν double meaning; πνεῦμα wind/Spirit. Confirm.
Nicodemus appears again at John 7:50 and 19:39; not mentioned here to keep one idea.
